# Webhook config (v1)

Schema for `.tera/webhooks/<name>.hcl` config files. Each decodes to `pkg/config.WebhookBlock`, an input-adapter that feeds inbound HTTP webhooks into the broker through the shared transform layer.

**The `webhook` block takes no label** — it is written `webhook { … }`. The names live one level down, on the nested `endpoint "<name>" {}` blocks, which are components of this block rather than resources of their own (ADR-087 D3). Several files may each declare one `webhook` block; they merge into a single composed block, and an endpoint name declared in two files is a merge conflict.

|---|---|
| Registry name | `config/webhooks` |
| Regime | persisted |
| Identity regime | `singleton` — the kind itself is the identity; neither the stem nor a label carries meaning (ADR-087 D3) |
| Current version | `v1` |
| Supported versions | `v1` |
| HCL block | `webhook` |
| Loader directory | `.tera/webhooks/<name>.hcl` |

| Served at | `GET /api/v1/schemas/config/webhooks/reference` |

## Example

A minimal `webhooks`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/webhooks/example-webhook.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

webhook {
  endpoint "example" {
    path        = "/hooks/example"
    output_type = "mqtt"

    mqtt {
      topic_expr = "ingress/v1/example"
    }
    response {
      mode = "fire-and-forget"
    }
  }
}
```

## `endpoint.verify_signature` block

Nested under `endpoint`.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `scheme` | string | yes | — | #1279 | — | Signature convention the producer uses. github-hmac-sha256 is GitHub's X-Hub-Signature-256 — HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body, lower-case hex, behind a sha256= prefix — and is what a Shopify- or Sentry-shaped producer means too. tera-hmac-sha256 is tera's own X-Tera-Webhook-Signature: the same MAC, bare hex, no prefix, and the least ceremony for a producer you control. slack-v0 is Slack's X-Slack-Signature — v0=<hex> of HMAC-SHA256 over v0:<X-Slack-Request-Timestamp>:<raw body> — and refuses a request without that timestamp header. A webhook listener judges no timestamp window and no replay under any scheme (#1279): slack-v0 here checks only that the timestamp was signed, so a captured Slack delivery re-sent later still verifies. |
| `secret` | string | yes | — | #1279 | — | Credential reference for the shared secret the producer signs with — env://VAR, keychain://service, vault://path, secret://row, or a literal. Re-resolved on a short timer rather than read once at boot, so rotating the secret does not need a daemon restart — it takes effect within seconds. Adding or changing the verify_signature block does not need one either: the endpoint set reconciles on reload (ADR-122 D1/D6), and the endpoint keeps its reply queue across the swap. Writing the secret itself here puts it in a vault file that is committed. |
